rows.speaker: all philologists
rows.claim: Philologists define ism as an expression conveying knowledge of a thing and distinguishing a substance, accident, or attribute; philosophically it is a concept.
rows.anchor: according to all philologists, an expression "conveying the knowledge [of a thing]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad infers that knowing all names means humans possess logical definition and conceptual thought.
rows.anchor: man's faculty of logical definition and, thus, of conceptual thinking

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adam represents the whole human race, as indicated by the angels' prior reference to corruption and bloodshed and by 7:11.
rows.anchor: the whole human race is meant here becomes obvious from the preceding reference

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels' claim was that their purity made them better qualified to inherit the earth.
rows.anchor: by virtue of their purity, were better qualified to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This passage continues the preceding discussion of the ongoing guidance given to humanity through revelation.
rows.anchor: continuous guidance vouchsafed to man through divine revelation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Israel is invoked because its religious beliefs were an earlier monotheistic phase, culminating in the Qur'anic revelation.
rows.anchor: their religious beliefs represented an earlier phase of the monotheistic concept which culminates in the revelation of the Qur'an

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses asks whether they would trade freedom for the meager comforts of Egyptian captivity; in Sinai they longed for Egypt's comparative security, as Numbers 11 and Moses' next sentence indicate.
rows.anchor: exchange your freedom for the paltry comforts which you enjoyed in your Egyptian captivity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Habata literally means descending a slope and figuratively falling in dignity; since Moses' exclamation is not literal, Asad combines both senses as returning to Egypt in shame.
rows.anchor: used figuratively in the sense of falling from dignity and becoming mean and abject

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage concerns a later phase of Jewish history; Asad cites John the Baptist and Gospel accusations by Jesus, plus accounts of Zachariah's murder, as evidence that Jews killed prophets.
rows.anchor: This passage obviously refers to a later phase of Jewish history.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The auxiliary kanu signals continuity or repeated persistence in their wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: implication of continuity in, or persistent repetition of, their wrongdoing transpires from the use of the auxiliary verb kanu

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before the qiblah revelation, the Prophet and community prayed toward the Ka'bah without a specific command; it was regarded as the first temple devoted to the One God despite its idols.
rows.anchor: used to turn in prayer towards the Ka'bah. This was not prompted by any specific revelation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the Prophet recognized Jerusalem's sanctity, he usually stood by the Ka'bah's southern wall, facing north toward both holy centers.
rows.anchor: the Prophet prayed, as a rule, before the southern wall of the Ka'bah, towards the north, so as to face both the Ka'bah and Jerusalem

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the move to Medina he prayed toward Jerusalem alone; about sixteen months later revelation definitively made the Ka'bah the Qur'an community's qiblah.
rows.anchor: definitively established the Ka'bah as the qiblah of the followers of the Qur'an

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Medina's Jews were displeased when Muslims abandoned Jerusalem, whose direction had pleased them.
rows.anchor: it is to them that the opening sentence of this passage refers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Historically, no divine qiblah command changed: no ordinance on direction of prayer existed before 2:142-150 was revealed.
rows.anchor: there had simply been no ordinance whatever in this respect before verses 142-150 were revealed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage connects to the preceding discussion of Abraham because he erected the earliest temple structure later known as the Ka'bah.
rows.anchor: Abraham who erected the earliest structure of the temple which later came to be known as the Ka'bah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad offers an alternate rendering in which God guides whoever wills to be guided onto a straight path.
rows.anchor: Or: "He guides onto a straight way him that wills [to be guided]"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A middlemost community balances extremes and realistically assesses human nature, rejecting both licentiousness and excessive asceticism.
rows.anchor: a community that keeps an equitable balance between extremes and is realistic in its appreciation of man's nature and possibilities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'anic moderation avoids overemphasis on bodily and material life while treating human physical urges and desires as legitimate because God willed them.
rows.anchor: man's urges and desires relating to this "life of the flesh" are God-willed and, therefore, legitimate

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase summarizes Islam's rejection of an inherent conflict between spirit and flesh and its affirmation of their natural, God-willed unity.
rows.anchor: a denial of the view that there is an inherent conflict between the spirit and the flesh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This balanced outlook flows from God's oneness and the unity of purpose underlying creation, making the community reference a fitting introduction to the Ka'bah as a symbol of oneness.
rows.anchor: the unity of purpose underlying all His creation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Muslim community should make its way of life an example for all humanity, just as the Apostle is an example for Muslims.
rows.anchor: that your way of life be an example to all mankind, just as the Apostle is an example to you

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Those whom God has guided are those to whom He has given understanding.
rows.anchor: whom He has given understanding" (Razi)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The qiblah change was a hard test because Muslims accustomed to Jerusalem, associated with earlier prophets, were asked to face the Ka'bah, then a pagan Quraysh shrine; the guided recognized Abraham's Temple as a symbol of oneness and Islamic unity.
rows.anchor: the Ka'bah, which at that time (in the second year after the hijrah) was still used by the pagan Quraysh as a shrine dedicated to the worship of their numerous idols

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hajj occurs once yearly in Dhu'l-Hijjah, while umrah may be performed at any time.
rows.anchor: The Mecca pilgrimage (hajj) takes place once a year, in the month of Dhu'l-Hijjah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both rites require seven circuits around the Ka'bah and seven trips between Safa and Marwah; hajj also requires attendance at Arafat on Dhu'l-Hijjah 9.
rows.anchor: pilgrims are required to walk seven times around the Ka'bah and seven times between As-Safa and Al-Marwah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pilgrims must not cut or trim their hair from entering ihram until the pilgrimage or visit ends; people ill with an ailment requiring hair removal are exempt.
rows.anchor: refrain from cutting or even trimming the hair on their heads from the time they enter the state of pilgrimage (ihram) until the end of the pilgrimage

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The offering reaching its destination can mean arrival at the appointed place or at the appointed time.
rows.anchor: in time or in place

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi takes the destination as the time of sacrifice, at the pilgrimage's conclusion, when able pilgrims are expected to offer an animal and distribute most of its meat in charity.
rows.anchor: according to Razi, the time of sacrifice is meant here, namely, the conclusion of the pilgrimage

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idha amantum, literally when safe, includes safety from external danger such as war and from illness; hale and secure means the pilgrim can and intends to participate.
rows.anchor: refers here to safety both from external dangers (e.g., war) and from illness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The provision describes ending ihram for comfort between umrah and hajj; the pilgrim using it must sacrifice an animal at pilgrimage's end or fast ten days.
rows.anchor: an interruption, for the sake of personal comfort, of the state of pilgrimage (ihram) during the time intervening between the completion of an 'umrah and the performance of the hajj

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those not resident near the Sacred Mosque means people who do not permanently live in Mecca; locals cannot remain permanently in ihram.
rows.anchor: do not permanently reside there: for, obviously, the inhabitants of Mecca cannot remain permanently in the state of ihram

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning covers every deliberate violation of God's ordinances, as well as possible violations of pilgrimage sanctity.
rows.anchor: not merely to a possible violation of the sanctity of the pilgrimage but also, in a more general way, to all deliberate violations of God's ordinances

rows.speaker: Ibn 'Abbas
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas's uncontested evidence identifies this as the Prophet's last revelation, received shortly before his death.
rows.anchor: According to the uncontested evidence of Ibn 'Abbas, the above verse was the last revelation granted to the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kalimah literally means word or utterance and is also used philosophically for a proposition or tenet.
rows.anchor: often used in the philosophical sense of "proposition" or "tenet"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since we refers to human beings, one another also means human beings, so people must not take each other as lords alongside God.
rows.anchor: the personal pronoun "we" obviously applies to human beings, the expression "one another" necessarily bears the same connotation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad applies the call to Christians who attribute divinity to Jesus and aspects of it to saints.
rows.anchor: not merely to the Christians, who attribute divinity to Jesus and certain aspects of divinity to their saints

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad also applies it to Jews who assign quasi-divine authority to Ezra and prominent Talmudic scholars.
rows.anchor: but also to the Jews, who assign a quasi-divine authority to Ezra and even to some of their great Talmudic scholars

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad identifies Jesus as the obvious referent and explains the sentence as saying that God grants a human revelation, judgment, and prophethood, after which he could not demand worship.
rows.anchor: This obvious reference to Jesus reads, literally, "It is not [possible] for a human being that God should grant him

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zamakhshari treats hukm, judgment or sound judgment, as synonymous here with hikmah, wisdom.
rows.anchor: Zamakhshari regards the term hukm ("judgment" or "sound judgment") occurring in the above sentence as synonymous

rows.speaker: Sibawayh (as quoted by Razi)
rows.claim: A rabbani is one devoted exclusively to knowing the Sustainer and obeying Him, a meaning close to man of God.
rows.anchor: According to Sibawayh (as quoted by Razi), a rabbani is "one who devotes himself exclusively to the endeavour to know the Sustainer (ar-rabb) and to obey Him"
